speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Last year, the hon Second Minister for Law lay emphasis on taking steps to secure our place in a post-COVID-19 world to ensure that we, as a country, will continue to thrive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This year, the hon Deputy Prime Minister in his Budget speech highlighted the need for resilience building to meet the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was the same point I made in the debate last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I advocated that we identify strategic areas to build resilience both in the short and long term, even if it means that we have to incur some extra costs and inefficiency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They drew on technology to provide online platforms for claimants, as well as public-spirited volunteers to be assessors of claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The end products – in the form of legislative solutions – has been widely admired for their elegance, simplicity in implementation and incisive thinking while meeting the ends of justice during a very trying period of time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The shape of these solutions, drawing as they do on general legal and policy principles, can be used again and again.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had previously suggested that we pass framework legislation that can be triggered, should our country face another similar crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Second Minister demurred, stating that each crisis is likely to be different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may be true, but the general principles are likely to be the same.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it would show that the chain of reasoning behind the legal structures which dealt with urgent and significant issues during the pandemic – these provide certainty and precedence for future events.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, it will show their practical impact and outcome, which will allow us to plan better for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thus, even though we have decided against framework legislation, the shape of what justice demands and confers during a pandemic is already known.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This predictability and the ability to extrapolate from past experiences confer real resilience to our legal system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to civil proceedings, I would like to ask for an update on the following matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister in 2022 said that his Ministry is working on it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the reform of the Civil Enforcement Framework.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, an update on the probate e-service system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had been advocating for this for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to community dispute management issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that, over the years, the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRT) is seeing a trend of increasing applications filed by persons who have disputes with their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I feel that it is useful to deploy professional mediation services on site, so that these persons are engaged at the earliest opportunity before the problems become more intractable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if the hon Minister feels that there is value in greater deployment of professional mediators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, I would be grateful if he could tell us how to increase our deployment of mediation services in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to Protection from Harassment Courts (PHCs).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The online Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS) has made it very easy for a person to lodge a claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst it is a good development, there are unintended drawbacks too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is possible for a person to lodge a completely unmeritorious claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because of the design feature of the system, such cases will still be registered, the defendants will still have to be served with the Court papers and they still have to be hauled into Court to answer the allegations which, on the face of it, are frivolous and vexatious.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such a situation, ironically, it is the claimant who is the harasser.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We want to make the costs of filing complaints low, but when the cost of filing frivolous claims is zero, it is an invitation to play games.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Has this been popular and if so, I wonder if there are any plans to enhance these services?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These may involve frequent loud noises, use of space along common corridors, inhalation of cigarette smoke wafting into a person's flat from a neighbour's flat and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats, the first port of call would usually be for HDB to intervene and speak to neighbours involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, HDB officers would often engage the neighbours and request for their cooperation and consideration by the resident who is the subject of complaint.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may work for some of the cases, but for many cases, the problems may not be resolved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some residents deliberately would not respond to mediation, I heard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If the matter cannot be resolved amicably, the dispute will continue to be adjudicated under the existing CDRT process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such process is not new to the Courts and has been around in the State Courts for a number of years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also suggest that to encourage a better attitude towards reasonable resolution, the attitude and conduct of parties at the mediation should be noted for purposes of the CDRT procedure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the procedure may already have been streamlined for easier filing and participation by laypeople, as compared to, say, our Court procedure for the State Courts, many are still intimidated by the procedural and the written evidential requirements, including even the demands of the initial claim filing requirements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are we able to reduce some of these formalities further?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Perhaps parties should be required to declare —

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: — at the onset that they have not engaged lawyers for assistance in any way.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Inevitably, there are cases where neighbours misunderstand each other and end up in disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In Singapore, I recognise that we have adopted both a legal and community solution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: On the legal front, we have the CDRT and CMC.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This is where our framework needs to have more bite to encourage compliance with the relevant orders and agreements.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In a recent engagement with Dr William Wan, Chairperson of the Community Advisory Panel on Neighbourhood Noise, what he told me echoed the need for more legal teeth, such as requiring mandatory attendance at mediations and to strengthen the enforcement of agreements between disputing neighbours.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: He highlighted the Government's successful implementation of table littering rules at hawker centres, noting the high compliance by individuals given the threat of a fine.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This example illustrates that a behavioural incentive model underpinned by legal sanctions can drive positive behaviour, leading to social benefits.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Separately, I also believe that the key to an effective implementation is by taking a more proactive stance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Thus, the introduction of a regime of trained on-the-ground councillors to actively engage parties involved in a community dispute at an early stage might facilitate the CDRT process.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In this regard, will MinLaw consider reviewing the existing framework to facilitate the use of persons with specialised knowledge to manage community disputes?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This has led to the in-flight of high-value multinational enterprises (MNEs) to establish their presence or headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This is key for Singapore's long-term growth and global presence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Singapore has become the choice jurisdiction for many, for the conduct of complex and high-value litigations and dispute resolution for MNEs and high net worth individuals.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: It is, therefore, key for businesses and individuals to be able to rely on Singapore's legal system, not just for swift justice, but also effective justice.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In this regard, there is scope for improvements in our legal enforcement framework.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: At the end of a civil litigation proceeding, it is usual for the Court to issue an Order or Judgment, for which it often involves a monetary sum known as the judgement sum.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This judgement sum is often not easy to enforce.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Therefore, it is not uncommon to hear corporates, as well as individuals, having trouble in enforcing these monies, which if not paid, makes this a paper judgement.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: I recognise that the Singapore Courts has in recent years, improved the judicial process related to civil procedures to facilitate access to justice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My first cut is on the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) and CDRT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since coming into force in November 2014, can MinLaw provide an update on POHA cases and the POHA Court that has been set up, especially the number of cases settled and adjudicated?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask for the POHA Court also to track the breakdown of the various types of POHA claims, for example, online versus offline, sexual harassment and workplace harassment cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I also wish to ask MinLaw to provide an update on CDRT cases and share the plans to better ensure the efficient and effective resolution of CDRT complaints, as there are more situations of work-from-home, resulting in more neighbourly disputes on the ground.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some of these disputes cannot be resolved via the voluntary mediation, via community mediation and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the event of a company undergoing insolvency process, even though there is a priority of debts prescribed by law, workers' outstanding wages remain unsecured debts and there is usually little to no assets left to pay these workers' salaries, after all the company's secured debts have been satisfied.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: An unpaid worker may still need to go through a protracted enforcement process against the company to recover unpaid salaries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is further exacerbated during recent times when companies undergo other related proceedings, such as judicial management, where a moratorium is ordered where we cannot enforce our rights under a collective agreement and other due process without leave of Court, which is an onerous, cumbersome and costly process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just this month, one of my Pioneer Single Member Constituency (SMC) residents came to see me at my Meet-the-People Session as he had unpaid wages and Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions for months because his company is undergoing judicial management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can MinLaw do something about this unfortunate situation?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chair, I have met Clementi residents who were litigants-in-person in family law proceedings; did not have a lawyer; and represented themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They found it very hard to find their way through the system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, I shared about my Clementi resident who wanted to vary a maintenance order after her divorce; litigant-in-person; did not have a lawyer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She told us that to submit a security deposit, she needed to go through VITAL, a department under the Ministry of Finance (MOF).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: By the time the certificate of security deposit was issued, she had missed the deadline for appeal – we were told.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She told us she had to liaise with CrimsonLogic, a service bureau which handled some of the transactions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister tell us what is the role of these additional intermediaries?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do they make it more complicated for laypersons who do not have resources of a law firm, especially persons who have limited resources, from the older generation, who might not be fluent in English?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What has been done since last year to make the journey less difficult for litigants-in-person in family law proceedings, especially Singaporeans who do not qualify for legal aid but do not earn enough to engage a lawyer?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chair, in the implementation of our system, we must make sure that due process does not present undue difficulties or undue obstacles because justice delayed, justice disrupted, justice complicated may become justice denied.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chair, the Legal Aid Bureau is an important pillar of the access to justice, providing legal advice to those with lower income.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Those who qualify for legal aid get free or low-cost legal representation and protection from adverse cost consequences if a decision goes against them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, there remains a significant cliff effect for those who fail to qualify for legal aid, since they will be on the hook for both legal fees and potential cost consequences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have encountered divorce cases where one party, usually the wife who is not working, qualifies for legal aid while the husband, who works but has a low-paying job, would not qualify for legal aid and ends up being unrepresented and at a disadvantage in the Court process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How well has the service been utilised so far?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are there any further improvements envisioned for legal aid?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the Legal Aid Bureau had provided assistance on civil matters for individuals who need assistance in criminal matters, it was the Law Society's Criminal Legal Aid Scheme that had provided this assistance for many years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Last year, in line with the announcement at the Committee of Supply (COS) debate, the Public Defender's Office (PDO) was launched, with the aim of providing assistance for criminal defence work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry can share how well utilised these services have been so far, including how many applications there were and how many have been provided with public defenders to represent them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Does the Ministry expect an increase to the numbers of people applying for public defence?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am not legally trained but I was supportive of the Government's move to set up the PDO to widen the ambit of providing access to legal representation for accused persons who are unable to afford it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Members of this House would have experienced many requests for legal advice, aid or representation by residents or families of residents who require them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the community, we have legal aid clinics or even lawyers – who are volunteers – who pitch in to give some guidance to residents who need legal assistance but are unable to pay the fees to retain a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many laypersons who have had the unfortunate need of having to deal with legal entanglements will tell you that it is not a pleasant experience.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In particular, if a person is charged with a crime, it does not affect only the accused but greatly impacts family members and dependents.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The situation is greatly aggravated if the family is from a lower-income household.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I hope that the PDO will achieve its overarching objective of supporting accused persons with limited means to be legally well advised and professionally represented.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As we usually say, the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We shall await to hear of the good work of the PDO.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share an update with this House on the PDO, in particular, on the number of applications received so far, the number of public defenders appointed and whether, at this early stage, we are seeing an increased number of applications for representation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government had been funding the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, now Pro Bono SG, for some years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Last month, I attended the launch of Pro Bono SG's Community Law Centre (CLC) in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Two lawyers are stationed full-time at CLC who are able to provide legal assistance to walk-ins on any legal matter, not just criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, CLC also works with a myriad of community organisations that they may refer these walk-ins to, in the event that the remedy may not be a legal one.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, Sir, is an important and valuable initiative that brings accessibility to legal advice, and ultimately to justice, right into the communities that may need it most, and not just on criminal matters – because people may face legal hurdles in many other areas of life, from family matters to harassment, and they may not know how to go about dealing with them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am told by Pro Bono SG that they have seen people coming to see them from as far away as Boon Lay.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government could consider continuing to provide funding to Pro Bono SG for more such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope to see more CLCs open up in more neighbourhoods in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government elaborate on how the PDO will continue to engage volunteer lawyers to ensure that the spirit of giving back continues to thrive in the industry, in particular as regards criminal aid?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Law firms of the future will be driven by technology, innovation and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How do our firms stand with regards to new areas of practice, like digital tokens and currencies, as well as rapidly evolving areas like intellectual property and data privacy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Ministry also consider a review of the Bar exam syllabus to incorporate how lawyers can use technology, such that it becomes native to lawyers right from the start, that lawyering requires knowledge of the technology-powered tools and applications.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such education should also include the correct ways that such technology should be harnessed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Chat GPT has many possible uses for lawyers, both good and bad.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having invested heavily on technology and digital solutions, my firm is one of those that have utilised technology during the period of pandemic to handle clients, commercial transactions and international arbitration cases all over the world, across time zones, adding to my eyebags.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This meant that our clients' needs are being met and the experience, training and exposure of lawyers, especially younger ones, continue despite the disruption of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, the Courts in Singapore, like the State Courts and Syariah Court, faced technical issues in Court document filing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, some firms lack the resources to keep pace with the ever-changing legal landscape, which gives a clear advantage of terrain to those who employ technological means.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The digital divide also gives an advantage to those who have the means to use technology – and those who have not.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is MinLaw supporting lawyers especially younger lawyers and those in small firms, to better meet the evolving needs of our society and economy?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can digitalisation be harnessed in the legal sector, to ensure that justice remains accessible to all, regardless of social economic standing?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And what are the steps and infrastructure that MinLaw is looking to set up to ensure that the Court electronic filing system and other processes can cope with the increasing caseload and future challenges?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the rise of Zoom and some work-from-home days, different skillsets and mindsets are required to adapt to new routines and norms.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cloud-based legal technology tools can be relied upon for document storage and communication.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, as more and more technology arise to assist the legal profession, how is MinLaw ensuring that the human element continues to be relevant?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a partnership between legal manpower and technology will contribute to Singapore's post-pandemic economic growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Chair, I declare my interest as Director of Legal for the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and honorary member of Singapore Corporate Counsel Association (SCCA).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In-house counsels in Singapore form a significant and growing part of our legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Well-skilled in-house counsels greatly boost the value and expertise of companies to confidently close deals, act in line with compliance practices and navigate risks in a complex and changing world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, we also have a group of para-legals, also known as para-professionals or legal executives in law firms and corporate entities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Many of them graduated from the Diploma in Legal Executive Studies or the Diploma in Law and Management by Temasek Polytechnic or other educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: When I last engaged this group of graduates, they also hope to build and boost their professionalism, competencies and standards, continuing education and career progression opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: They will, therefore, require further support from MinLaw in their drive towards this end.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How can MinLaw help to uplift and further enhance the in-house counsel and para-legal/para-professional fraternities through active support of their learning and skills development, as well as their career progression?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the pandemic, many of the challenges that lawyers had been facing bubbled to the fore, including burnout, career progression and work culture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Work from anywhere, coupled with constant communication, adds to the pressures of lawyering.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we move forward in a new era, how is MinLaw supporting both senior and junior lawyers to better meet the evolving legal needs of society and economy?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, many organisations operate on land which is leased to them by the Government for 30 years, and are subject to renewal thereafter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that some temples and churches find the sums charged for the issue and renewal of land leases to be very high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The sums they need to raise often require significant fund-raising efforts, which in turn take their energies away from their main mission of practising and propagating their faith.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that the Government is alive to these worries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has announced that it is reviewing its policy in this area and had been consulting religious groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The review has been going on for some months now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In answer to my Parliamentary Question filed in October last year, the Minister stated that state land parcels, including those allocated for Place of Worship use, were required to be sold at fair market value.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He explained that this meant that the parcels of land were generally sold through a competitive tender process, where the highest acceptable price becomes the land price for the specific site.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He attributed the rise in prices due to the competitive bidding process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the Government review of land allocation and pricing framework for land for places of worship is ongoing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Churches, mosques, temples, and other religious institutions are cornerstones of our communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They provide succour for the bereaved, counsel for the needy and guidance for the lost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many have operated in the communities that they serve for long periods of time – decades, and in some cases, centuries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this cost is not only high, but exorbitant for institutions that are not fundamentally profit-making in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the most successful of those operating with this model even build a "super C" – shopping centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I believe that it is unfair to expect every religious institution to engage in commerce; after all, some may hold the view that their earthly purpose is explicitly to reject such secular activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another alternative is to adopt the now-standard price quality method framework, which would place a greater weight on factors like the diversity of religious bodies in a given town, or the duration that a church or mosque or temple has served in a given community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I explained during the HDB debate, the Government already differentially prices land for different classes and uses of that land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These suggestions simply extend that logic to religious institutions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Although the interim use of land is being applied, their tenures tend to be not more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This limits the amount of investments that can be made into such lands or properties, therefore also limiting the range and quality of interim uses.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I am mindful that entrenchment of interim uses can also impede long-term flexibility.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Would it help if we supplement our master plan with an interim use plan that could guide land use on say 15, 30 and 45 years usage?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore has about 730 square kilometres of land, and that scarcity has always pushed us to innovate and stretch our land options.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have done very well to reclaim land and build upwards and downwards to maximise use of our land.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One other solution is to reuse state properties by converting underutilised plots of land into community spaces.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Additionally, many existing plots of land have been converted into areas for Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: More such spaces are necessary in our dense city to create spaces for people to exercise, view nature and spend time with family and friends.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Given the limited land resources in Singapore, and considering our desire to preserve as much of our natural greenery as possible, how has MinLaw continued to seek out state properties that may be repurposed and rejuvenated for the community?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: It is essential that land use and state properties are optimised for the community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How does SLA decide which properties are selected, on what timelines and are there any upcoming plans that the public can look forward to?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: In November last year, I briefly spoke about the upkeep and protection of the SLA-managed lands, such as the Southern Islands.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Given the multitude of recreational and research activities on these islands, does SLA have any plans to work with other agencies in enhancing the frameworks and protections of these islands, for example, through zoning?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: SLA has also been developing other state‐of‐the‐art geospatial data management, analytic and delivery technologies.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Having ready access to trustworthy and spatially explicit information is more important now than ever to help us address climate change, sustainability and other emerging challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: What are the Government's plans to mainstream and leverage Singapore's geospatial capabilities, to inform and support policies, decisions and actions across all segments of Singapore society?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is competing demand for the limited land to be used for residential, industrial, commercial, roads and parks.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Given the limited land resources in Singapore, it is important that the state maximise the best use of its available resources.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I had previously suggested that we consider the car park space at sports stadiums to be used for parking by heavy commercial vehicles at night when the stadium is not being used.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This could free up some space for heavy vehicles or commerical vehicles to park.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, during off-peak hours, when there are no sporting activities at the stadium, the carpark is generally empty.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why can the state not allow better use of this empty car park space?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We should look at different options to better make use of scarce land.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is a vacant piece of state land next to Haig Court which has been vacant for some years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Today, there are many people involved in the conveyancing process – lawyers, secretaries, clerks, agents and bankers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Their role is to ensure that parties, who are buying properties or assets worth millions of dollars, are properly protected and they are able to obtain title to the assets that they agree to buy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am unclear as to what the digital conveyancing portal means for conveyancing lawyers, clerks, agents and bankers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Option to purchase are contractual terms to be negotiated between buyers and sellers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For title to properties, there are many leasehold properties being transacted.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
