text: What are the steps that MinLaw have in mind to raise public awareness of the use and benefits of the DCP when fully implemented?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Spurred by profound developments in the world, including all the experiences that Members have spoken about – geopolitical tensions; reconfiguration of economic value chains; technological developments; sustainability and climate change; and of course, the recently passed COVID-19 pandemic of which we have seen the worst of, and hopefully, we have put it behind us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And within Singapore as well, an ageing population and an increasingly educated and skilled workforce.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All of these factors intertwined together, developing and reshaping the way we live, work and also interact with one another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To ensure that Singapore continues to thrive amidst these changes, the MinLaw is working on various fronts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The scope – as you can see from the breadth of topics raised by Members – is diverse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Increasing access to justice; enhancing legal processes; optimising land utilisation and promoting land data; assisting businesses with protecting their intangible assets and intellectual property; and finding a platform for this to be commercialised and leveraged, for the industry to grow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst the work is wide-ranging, our vision is singular: bettering people's lives, creating value jobs, advancing our economy and society, through laws and policies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That ultimately, is the bottom line and the top line of what we do at MinLaw.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, perhaps, is best encapsulated by our responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, which Mr Murali Pillai – thank you very much – commended.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These measures covered a broad range of issues, such as: adjusting contractual obligations, providing rental relief and supporting distressed entities through insolvency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of these steps unprecedented and novel, but also highly necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Pillai said we could chronicle our efforts as we went through these different challenges to deal with the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving forward, my Ministry will work along three broad thrusts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, enhancing the trust, relevance and accessibility of our legal system for society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, contributing to and supporting economic activity in Singapore – by identifying and seizing new opportunities in the legal and intellectual property sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And third, optimising and rejuvenating our land and properties for the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue in this vein to drive reforms and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu will elaborate on these programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members are aware, an interagency committee led by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), together with the Ministry of National Development (MND), is conducting a comprehensive review of the CDMF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The goal is threefold: first, to encourage pro-social behaviour; second, to facilitate amicable resolution of disputes between neighbours; and third, to deal with this as far as possible, at an early stage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To achieve this, we are looking at enhancements in three broad areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, as I said, early intervention – by building consensus through community norms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will set shared expectations on acceptable community behaviours; set out standards to help shape this normative behaviour in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will share more details of this when she speaks at MND's COS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, and I think we all know this; despite setting these norms and having these standards in the community, nuisance might still occur.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, very often, it will likely still occur.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The overall aim is to encourage, as far as possible, conciliation between neighbours, as much as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the appropriate cases, personnel from this team may conduct investigations to understand the nature and the root cause of the problem, and might require, in the right cases, residents to attend a mandatory mediation and also require them to stop the actions that are causing the nuisance, pending mediation or resolution downstream by the CDRT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More details of this process will be shared in MND and MCCY's COS in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even as we look at steps to enhance and improve this process, I said earlier that we intend to channel as much of these disputes as possible, through the mediated conciliatory route.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That, I think, we all accept, is the best way of resolving a neighbour dispute.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, given that, there will be a number of these intransigent cases, we will work towards strengthening the powers and the processes of the CDRT – which some Members spoke about – so that it can provide faster and more effective relief in the appropriate cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mediation can preserve and often even strengthen the relationship between neighbours by providing them with a platform, in the hands of a very well-trained mediator, to resolve their disputes amicably, in very much a win-win fashion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our experience has shown us that mediation is not just more effective, it is also quicker and cheaper.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The data shows that mediation has been, by and large, successful.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We, therefore, believe that most community dispute cases will benefit from mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This number, of course, has got to be taken in context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is for parties who voluntarily go to mediation, so they might, perhaps, be more predisposed to having an amicable resolution between themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, this statistic tells us that putting cases through mediation, at least as the first port of call, will likely yield effective results.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part of the problem is that these voluntary cases handled at CMC represent a minority of the cases as many neighbours do not make this attempt at mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, of all cases that go to the CMC on neighbour disputes – usually on noise – less than 30% go on to voluntary mediation and of this, 80% of that number of cases are resolved amicably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, as I said earlier, could in part be because mediation is currently voluntary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, if you are required to go through a mandatory mediation and you do not, then the case will not proceed at CDRT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, for voluntary mediation cases previously mediated and settled at CMC, but the mediated issues have resurfaced, or there is a new dispute related to what was mediated previously, CMC will be able to mandate re-mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, as I said earlier, we will, in general, require disputing neighbours to undergo mediation before they file a case at CDRT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will prevent disputes from unnecessarily escalating to a Court process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: After we make mediation mandatory, the 80% figure that I said earlier may well come down, it may not be as high because you will now be including in this group of mediated cases, those cases where parties do not want or do not wish to find a solution amongst themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, it is important to provide parties with that platform to seek an amicable resolution; and it can still be highly effective in the hands of a good mediator, and with some public education.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many Members in this House, as Mr Dennis Tan said earlier, have seen many of these cases in the course of their rounds when they visit their residents and their encouragement to refer these to mediation will help.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will set out those conditions after we have studied that and introduced these.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Pillai's query on forward deploying mediation services, you know what the answer is likely to be.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We believe that in the hands of a good mediator, many of these disputes can be resolved very amicably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In many cases, part of the reluctance to go to mediation is because you are having a dispute with your neighbour three feet away and you do not want to get into a bus all the way down to the Central Business District about 45 minutes away, to do the mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we believe in that it is a question of manpower, but I am pleased to share that CMC has begun offering mediation services at six satellite locations at selected ServiceSG Centres and also Community Clubs, some place within the precinct where the two neighbours are living or at least close by.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also offer online mediation for suitable voluntary neighbour dispute cases in two Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) as a pilot to start with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we will decide how it works and, perhaps, look at scaling that up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it removes – it sounds odd to say that in the context of Singapore – the geographical difficulties that they might face in trying to go down to a mediation when the party that they really should be speaking to is just three feet away.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To support these efforts, the CMC has begun to increase the number of mediators on its panel of accredited community mediators and will look at growing this pool as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Despite what I have said, some disputes will remain unresolved despite early intervention and best efforts at mediation and with all the efforts that we make at making mediation more accessible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MND's initiatives, which Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will speak about later, will complement the mediation and the CDRT process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lastly, we are also taking steps to ensure that residents are, in fact, aware of and have the resources to utilise these tools to help themselves resolve these disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Residents may have questions such as: what is mediation?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Or how do I explain my concerns to the mediator?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And, perhaps, how do I prepare for a CDRT hearing?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are, thus, working with partners in our community to provide residents facing such disputes with advice and guidance; and possibly also, legal representation in the more complex cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For the first time, full-time community lawyers will serve the community through the CLCs, providing legal advice and assistance on a whole range of different issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Thomas' point on the CLCs, Pro Bono SG does indeed have plans to expand the CLCs beyond the pilot that is currently at Tian De Temple.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are supportive of the work that they do, and the Government will assess at an appropriate juncture how best to support this expansion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continue to push ahead in enhancing Singapore's hard-earned position and reputation as a leading legal services and IP hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, I think, Members will appreciate is necessary, not just to grow the legal and IP sectors, but also to support Singapore's broader status as a centre for commerce, banking and finance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But as Members have noted, there will be challenges ahead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain, Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin pointed out, our society and our economy are evolving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will have an impact on our legal needs, and consequently, on law firms and lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Thomas noted, law firms are being disrupted by technology and innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas asked about the progress of the initiatives under the Professional Services ITM.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will be providing more details of the refreshed ITM during their COS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Technology has changed how judicial and legal services are delivered and consumed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our Courts and law firms need to equip themselves with the necessary tools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Courts have put in place measures to ensure that the case management systems can deal with an increasing caseload – a comment raised by Mr Zhulkarnain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Courts have various electronic filing systems to deal with different types of cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Each of these case management systems are constantly reviewed and enhanced, where necessary, to ensure that they meet the caseload.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The product teams for each system also track the utilisation rates of the servers, to anticipate necessary hardware and software upgrades, and also the occasional surge in demand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This approach, by and large, has served the Courts well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: While there are occasional disruptions due to unforeseeable hardware failures, software and servers are progressively being shifted to the latest cloud infrastructure to reduce such occurrences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where future challenges are concerned, the Courts have planned various enhancements to cater for an increasing need to allow citizens to file applications directly, so that they can cut out the intermediary process and be able to do so on their own.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Together with other efforts, the Courts are ready to meet future challenges and will continue regular dialogue with stakeholders, to better address user needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For law firms, we recognise it will be challenging for them, especially the small and medium-sized Singapore Law Practices (SLPs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is more difficult for them to curate, customise and, perhaps, develop their own IT solutions, mainly due to the lack of economies of scale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw has, therefore, taken on this role and launched the Legal Technology Platform (LTP) in July last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The LTP is a matter management and collaboration tool, customised for legal workflows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, developed to fit intuitively the legal workflow process that each firm, particularly a smaller firm, might need and require at the backend and it progressively also deals with needs at the front end.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Through the LTP, SLPs can manage and collaborate on matters more seamlessly internally and also with their clients externally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can also access data from commonly used practice and document management systems, such as Tessaract, Clio, TessaCloud and NetDocuments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas asked about the reception of the LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This firm is Albakri LLC, a small SLP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Instead of copying and pasting from past Microsoft (MS) Word documents, the firm created its own matter templates and listed all the tasks relevant to a particular matter on the LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This enables its new associates to familiarise themselves independently with the firm's processes and workflow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It not only frees up the partners' time to supervise and train the associates, but also helps to institutionalise the firm's know-how and knowledge bank.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And seeing its usefulness, the firm has also contributed a matter template on probate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is now publicly available through the LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, firms after seeing how it works for them, can decide that it wants to contribute a template, which will then be shared across on LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Other firms can access this and, eventually, level up using these best practices that are shared on the LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving forward, we plan to enhance the LTP with more features desired by SLPs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have constantly taken soundings from them to check on how they have used it, and what else they would like to see.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To complement the LTP, we have worked with the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and our industry partners to develop the Legal Industry Digital Plan (IDP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an additional resource, to guide SLPs on how the LTP and other tools work together complementarily to support their digital transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will also provide guidance on how SLPs can shore up their cybersecurity and data protection measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second aspect I want to speak about is manpower development – a point touched on by Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Zhulkarnain, Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Thomas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members have recognised, technology is an enabler.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It helps our law firms and our lawyers to work more efficiently and effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But it cannot replace human beings; it cannot replace the human lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, in family and criminal cases, where we are dealing with a range of emotions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it is not just the legal considerations or what the law might say, but what are those special, peculiar idiosyncrasies and emotions that go behind each decision that might be made, particularly in family and criminal matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In complex cases, where we are dealing with different contexts, different nuances and, perhaps, also in the context of business done in Singapore or through Singapore, the Asian way of doing business context and the particular experience that a lawyer has with his or her client, all that is not something that an AI, like a chatbot, can easily replicate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, ChatGPT, the most invoked chatbot tool that we have seen in recent times, it did pass the law exams with a C+.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Reports say that it may be helpful at producing a first draft for lawyers to consider but, as I said, it does not deal with the range of emotions that might lie behind why a client might choose a certain course of action, in a range of cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it will also struggle with the most classic components of law exams, such as spotting the potential legal issues and also the deep analysis of applying the legal rules to the particular situation and nuances of the particular case, and also appreciate the human dynamics and personal idiosyncrasies which may lie behind even the most complex of complex corporate transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also exploring exchange programmes with foreign Bar associations, with the objective being to help Singapore lawyers build networks externally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Because of globalisation, transactions are now very much cross-border and relations that we develop with other lawyers from other jurisdictions will give our lawyers a leg-up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will also gain a deeper understanding of the work in priority markets through overseas attachments or study visit opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, let me touch on legal education reforms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will take into account the evolving needs of our society and economy – very much the various points raised by Members earlier about taking onboard today's context, evolving needs, what we foreshadow and forecasts that we might need for tomorrow's profession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will include areas of practice which are new, emerging or growing, for example, in technology and civil law, and applies to law schools and also to continuing professional development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas suggested reviewing the Bar exam syllabus to incorporate harnessing technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Based on feedback from the industry, the current generations of law students are generally technologically-savvy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, as part of the Singapore Institute of Legal Education's (SILE) recent review of the Part B Syllabus, contemporary legal issues, such as law and technology, and the use of technology in practice have also been incorporated to better prepare candidates for practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will, no doubt, equip law students and lawyers as well with the knowledge and skills they need for practice, and prepare them for the challenges ahead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will hopefully allow them to develop a more sustainable career in the legal industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is a lot of stress, whether it is from clients and sometimes, from Judges when you appear in Court, and fellow practitioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As the President of the Law Society, Mr Adrian Tan, noted in his speech at the OLY, in 2022, it had its first membership reduction in half a decade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I looked at the numbers that Mr Tan cited.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He cited them as of 31 August 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Shortly before that, a batch of new lawyers for the year were mass called, introduced and called to the Bar.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, when we looked at the trends and did a more granular review, it is apparent that, although it is increasing, but the rate of increase of the number of qualified practising lawyers has come down.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it is increasing but the rate of increase has slowed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And, in part, this is due to a decrease in the number of returning overseas law graduates, and also, as Mr Tan pointed out, an increase in attrition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But at the same time, I would say attrition from private practice is not new.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those of us who are lawyers and have been in practice for a while, would have seen the trend, even from before.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers now – in fact, today – have more options than in the past and can leave private practice but still contribute within the legal sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And like Mr Patrick Tay said earlier, greatly boosting legal services as in-house corporate counsel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the lawyers who leave practice carry with them that experience from practice into these other fields which are adjunct to practice but also serving the legal industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not necessarily a bad outcome, because we need legal talent to support all aspects of our economy and our society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin referred to young lawyers experiencing burnout.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Making private practice sustainable is something which the Government cannot alone achieve.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has got to be working with bodies like the Singapore Academy of Law, Law Society and even firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it requires effort from all of these parties because the work environment, we know, has a direct impact on the well-being of lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I am heartened to note that, on this score, the Law Society has a number of support schemes available for mentorship, guidance on career-related issues, or support with stress management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example is the Members' Assistance and Care Helpline, a one-stop referral and information service that Law Society members can turn to when faced with issues at work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our efforts also extend to other professionals within the legal industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how we are supporting them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For in-house counsel, we work closely with the SCCA, of which Mr Patrick Tay is an honorary member, to promote community building and to roll out training and development initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Examples include a mentorship programme and courses for targeted upskilling for corporate counsel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw also supports training providers in the development of programmes that build up capabilities of the legal community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are also made available to in-house counsel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For paralegals, we are studying how paralegals can take on more functions to support the work of lawyers and law firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is part of the legal education reforms that the Working Group, which I mentioned earlier, is also studying.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was to take effect from 2023 session of the Part B of the Singapore Bar Examination onwards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, MinLaw noted feedback from the industry that the COVID-19 pandemic, work from home and other such measures, had caused disruptions to work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More information will be available from MinLaw and other stakeholders in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our world is evolving, in no small part, because of digitalisation and new technologies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This heightens the importance of protecting intangible assets (IA) and intellectual property (IP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, let me share our IP strategy, which aims to prepare our businesses as they digitalise and innovate in the global economy, which is intrinsically linked with IA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIPS 2030 is a 10-year blueprint to strengthen and cement Singapore's position as a global IA and IP hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intention is to provide a consistent basis for businesses to disclose and communicate details of their intangibles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A framework, so that everyone speaks the same language and can understand what that disclosure is meant to describe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will provide stakeholders with comparable information about the businesses' intangibles, so that more informed assessments of the business and financial prospects can be made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will, in turn, facilitate intangible asset commercialisation, transactions and financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government is aware of these issues, as Ms Lim had noted in her speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have given our response previously, and we have been looking at this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as Members would appreciate, this has been the subject of very careful study, given its implications on land allocation and pricing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This study is still ongoing, and details will be released when we have completed the study.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is so that these organisations would not be compromised by entering into a long-term lease arrangement on the present framework before the review is completed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our legal system is a cornerstone of society that allows us to thrive economically and maintain order and justice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MinLaw is, therefore, committed to bringing a better quality of life for our people through enhancements to the legal system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, I will elaborate on efforts to increase access to justice, support individuals navigating family justice processes, make enforcement of judgments cheaper and easier, and utilise technology to enhance legal processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Being able to access the legal system is a pillar of the rule of law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, supporting vulnerable groups that require legal assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides the Community Law Centre that Minister Tong shared, there are other forms of legal aid and assistance provided by non-Government partners, some of which are available to foreigners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are about 70 legal clinics run by various community, religious and voluntary welfare organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For instance, the Migrant Worker Legal Clinics was launched by Pro Bono SG, in partnership with other members of the Migrant Workers' Group.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MinLaw is also working with Pro Bono SG and others to develop a one-stop portal to provide legal information and connect users to additional resources and assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It will also enable better coordination of legal clinics, such that legal advice will be more accessible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We welcome Mr Raj Joshua Thomas' comments and will continue to strengthen the network of support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, we continually review Singaporeans' level of access to legal help and representation in Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For civil legal aid, since 1958, the Government has been delivering aid to deserving cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For criminal legal aid, the broad principle, for a long time, was that the Government should not pay to defend accused persons, except in capital cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the years, we have moved to fund a part of the costs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2015, the Government started funding the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) directly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Last year, the Government decided to do more, establishing the PDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Responding to Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Mr Thomas, I am glad to share that the PDO has started off smoothly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The PDO also collaborates closely with Pro Bono SG to co-deliver criminal defence aid, ensuring it is administered efficiently and that we minimise duplication.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, all applications for criminal defence aid by Singaporeans and Permanent Residents (PRs) are assessed by PDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Then, there is a two-step process that determines which cases go to PDO or CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The remaining bulk of cases are shared between PDO and CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The actual cases will be assigned based on the relative workload and capacity of PDO and CLAS, to ensure resources of both are used efficiently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With the increase in coverage, we expect that volunteer lawyers will continue to play a role in ensuring justice is accessible to all segments of society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government's partnership with CLAS will help to preserve the pro bono spirit of the legal fraternity, which remains a key pillar of legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will conduct a review of the criminal defence aid system at an appropriate juncture to determine how to leverage the strengths of CLAS and the PDO in the long term.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As it has only been three months since its establishment, we will continue to monitor the caseload of the PDO closely to see that there is adequate staffing and capacity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We had increased the criminal defence aid income threshold, as a study conducted by MinLaw showed that households around the 35th percentile will find it challenging to afford legal representation before the Courts, even for plead guilty cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On the civil legal aid means test criteria, we had recently revised the criteria in end-2019.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will review the civil legal aid means test criteria in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I turn to family justice, an area that has a deep impact on the lives of individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Divorce Assets Informative Division Estimator (Divorce AIDE) was launched in September 2022.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is an online tool aimed at improving access to legal services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Divorce AIDE educates users on how matrimonial assets are generally divided upon divorce, and the estimated share and amount they are likely to receive from the matrimonial assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Its algorithm provides an indication of a reasonable range that parties can receive from the pool of matrimonial assets, post-divorce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Parties can use this to consider whether to settle the division of matrimonial assets amicably.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On Mr Murali Pillai's query as to whether the needs of the children are taken into account by the algorithm, this will have to be separately considered when negotiating a settlement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Children's needs are particular to each family and cannot be easily reduced to an algorithm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For instance, if there are children with special needs, parties may consider not dividing the insurance policies and setting them aside for the children's benefit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the children need to stay near their schools, selling the matrimonial flat may not be the most viable option.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moreover, on the day-to-day needs, their monthly expenses would be more appropriately dealt with by fixing child maintenance, as opposed to assets division.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Divorce AIDE has received positive feedback from social workers, Judges and our partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, feedback from the Community Justice Centre (CJC) noted it is "very easy to use"; "helpful in explaining and answering my questions on divorce"; and "an outstanding tool that litigants-in-person will find useful".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will refine Divorce AIDE in the upcoming year, a point mentioned by Mr Nair.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, we will collect more feedback to see how the tool has been useful and how it can be further improved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, we are exploring possible integration with MyInfo.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If successful, this will provide a more seamless experience, as users' Central Provident Fund (CPF) and HDB information may be extracted directly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are various forms of support for self-represented persons (SRPs) who commence, or wish to commence, proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng shared how his resident, an SRP, had to approach CrimsonLogic and VITAL.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He asked about the role of these intermediaries, and if they complicate the process for SRPs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, the Judiciary's case filing system, eLitigation, enables lawyers with a subscription to e-file documents and pay filing fees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SRPs can approach the CrimsonLogic Service Bureau, who will assist them with their e-filing and collect the filing fees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, SRPs generally do not interact with VITAL.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SRPs only interact with VITAL when a Court deposit is required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, when an SRP files an appeal, he or she is required to provide security for costs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SRPs would have to deposit the security with the Accountant-General, with VITAL acting as its collecting agent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To make these processes more convenient for SRPs, several initiatives have been rolled out, and others are in the pipeline.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Amongst other things, the e-service uses guided questions to assist applicants in filling up Court forms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is also integrated with MyInfo, which allows an applicant's particulars to be automatically populated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will be applicable to the large majority of uncontested probate cases, such as those involving a single executor and with lesser quantum of assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For other applications, the CrimsonLogic Service Bureau has been re-sited from Chinatown Point to the one-stop service hubs in the Supreme Court and State Courts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SRPs can file applications via the Service Bureau, access case management systems from self-help terminals, and carry out related Court processes from a single location.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As for putting up security for costs, FJC has published an online guide on the procedure for doing so and VITAL's contact information.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Furthermore, VITAL has allowed SRPs to make e-payments since 2020.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng raised the issues of delays in VITAL processing payments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This ensures that any delay in processing the payment or issuing the receipt does not result in an appellant missing out on the filing deadlines.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides these enhancements, there are two further areas that we have worked on, to make family justice more accessible to SRPs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, we try to ensure information on Court processes and procedures is readily available.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Courts publish on their website comprehensive information about Court processes and procedures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: FJC also published a case management guidebook which guides SRPs through the divorce process and a guidebook on common family Court orders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For those not fluent in English, digital and physical brochures on family law and Court processes in vernacular languages are available at the Judiciary's website and at FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Where more explanation is needed, SRPs can seek help from the Community Justice Centre (CJC) located within the premises of the State Courts and FJC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, there are online tools and resources that SRPs may find useful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides Divorce AIDE that I mentioned earlier, the Legal Aid Bureau's iLAB chatbot provides tailored legal information on divorce, family violence, and issues related to employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is also able to generate simple legal documents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the past year, information on civil cases was added to iLAB.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Responding to Mr Murali Pillai, iLAB is useful for users who have little to no legal knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Users have also given feedback that iLAB saves time and is convenient to use.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue collating feedback to improve iLAB.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The efforts to enhance access to justice in family proceedings is a continuing one.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The proposed changes aim to build on our efforts to reduce acrimony in family proceedings and ensure a fair outcome without undue complexity and costs for the parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This increases access to justice for litigants, especially those who cannot afford legal representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Non-compliance with maintenance orders has an adverse impact on those who are relying on the maintenance payments to go about their daily lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Unresolved disputes over maintenance also hinder the parties from moving forward with their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Upon divorce, the ex-husband was ordered to make monthly maintenance payments to Ms B for the two children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: After a few months, the ex-husband began missing payments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At one point, he had failed to make payment for more than five months.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The situation caused Ms B great distress – she had to cover the substantial costs of the children's school fees, transport and daily necessities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In less than a year, Ms B filed two applications to enforce the maintenance order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She had to spend considerable time and was unable to afford a lawyer to aid her in the proceedings, given her financial responsibilities to her children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The proposed reforms will make the enforcement of maintenance orders simpler and more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, in the current process, parties have to make several trips to court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The reforms aim to streamline proceedings and reduce the number of trips that parties make to Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will reduce the burden on those without lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will provide more details in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Next, the Protection from Harassment Court (PHC) was established to provide simplified, expedited processes to enhance access to justice for harassment victims.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Responding to Mr Patrick Tay, the data is encouraging.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Anecdotally, the majority of cases are handled by the litigants, without the need for legal representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There has been a significant increase in the number of PO applications, as well as orders granted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: From 2019 to 2020, 319 PO applications were filed; 146 POs were granted in that period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Applications may be withdrawn because parties reached an out-of-Court resolution, or the claimant decided there is no longer a need for a PO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The remaining 209 PO applications are either pending resolution or were dismissed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Where urgent relief is sought, the PHC generally hears the application within two to three working days from the date of application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Tay asked for a breakdown of the types of cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Members should note that one case may involve more than one type of harassment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Pillai resurfaced his proposal from last year to amend the PHC rules to summarily determine and dispose of frivolous and vexatious claims, without notifying the respondent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As explained in a written reply to Mr Pillai's question in Parliament previously, as part of due process, the Courts will usually require the respondent's side of the story to determine whether the claim is indeed frivolous or vexatious.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should also be mindful that many claimants in the PHC are SRPs, so the bar cannot be placed too high.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Otherwise, this could inadvertently prevent access to justice for them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On the other hand, the PHC has powers to deal with frivolous or vexatious cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For claims filed through simplified proceedings, the PHC has powers to make such orders and directions as it thinks fit for the just, expeditious and economic disposal of a case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The PHC therefore may, notwithstanding that the proceedings were already simplified, deal with a case which is frivolous, vexatious, or otherwise an abuse of process in an expedited way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For claims filed through standard proceedings, the normal procedures in the Rules of Court, such as striking out, are available.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Further, the PHC can award costs and disbursements against a claimant who brings a frivolous or vexatious case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This should deter any litigant who thinks they can misuse the PHC's simplified processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This prevents such a claimant from commencing actions or applications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Various stakeholders, including the Judiciary, are pulling in the same direction to enhance access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will provide an even greater emphasis and focus on access to justice from a Whole-of-Judiciary perspective.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Office will coordinate access to justice efforts across the Courts, review existing citizen-facing services and processes, and embark on new projects to improve the experience of Court users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For a start, some areas of focus will include enhancing accessibility to information, integrating services for the greater convenience of Court users, and improving the overall end-to-end service experience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I turn to upcoming changes to strengthen Singapore's legal system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As mentioned by Mr Pillai and Mr Derrick Goh, MinLaw has been studying possible reforms to the civil enforcement framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MinLaw's project focuses on making enforcement cheaper and easier, so that those who have succeeded in their claims, are not denied their fruits simply because they feel enforcement is too complex or expensive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will go some way towards alleviating the difficulties faced by judgement creditors today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More broadly, these reforms will ensure Singapore's legal system remains robust, efficient and business-friendly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will, in turn, help to preserve Singapore's status as a dispute resolution hub, a point raised by Mr Goh.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The proposed reforms, which affect enforcement of all civil judgements, are complex and may have far-reaching changes that have to be studied carefully.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have been working closely, over the past year, with the Judiciary and other stakeholders to refine the proposals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I would highlight technology is an integral aspect in many of our initiatives, as it strengthens access to the legal system – a perspective mentioned by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will, in a short while, mention how we are using technology to optimise state land.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will provide greater convenience to lawyers and their clients.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Lastly, I would like to address two points.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Patrick Tay touched on workers of insolvent companies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This issue has been addressed on numerous occasions in this House.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Exposure to business risks is something all companies face.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When these risks eventuate and a company gets into trouble, a restructuring aims to provide the company space to recover.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court supervises the restructuring process to balance the interests of the various stakeholders, including employees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the company is successfully rehabilitated, workers are more likely to hold on to their jobs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the restructuring is unsuccessful and the company enters into insolvent winding up, section 203 of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act gives priority to certain claims.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The only categories with priority over worker claims are the costs and expenses of winding up.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are necessary for the winding up to proceed smoothly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In fact, worker claims rank above claims by the Government, in respect of tax assessed and goods and services tax due.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Tay highlights insolvent companies having insufficient assets to pay workers even with the statutory priority scheme, and difficulties faced by workers in dealing with judicial managers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: That said, lower wage workers with unpaid salaries may receive financial assistance from the Short-term Relief Fund and the Migrant Workers' Assistance Fund.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Such assistance is also available where companies are not insolvent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Marshalling and allocating resources, including to employees to keep the business going, would depend very much on the specific facts and circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Pillai asked about Singapore's planned accession to the Hague Service Convention.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am pleased to update that we have been actively working on amendments to the relevant pieces of legislation to give effect to our obligations under the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We aim to introduce the amendments by the fourth quarter this year, at the same time when the Convention enters into force for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Lastly, I move to our initiatives to optimise land use and related matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At the outset, we are focused on helping Singapore and its people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With our limited land, we need to constantly innovate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is not innovating for its own sake, but with the goal of improving the quality of lives and building vibrant spaces and communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are, thus, pressing ahead on the digitalisation of the conveyancing process, evolution and mainstreaming of geospatial technologies, and rejuvenation of state lands.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have embarked on, in my view, an exciting project – the Digital Conveyancing Portal, or DCP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of us would have probably experienced the conveyancing process, which currently takes a rather manual approach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will soon be a thing of the past as the SLA brings to fruition its vision of the DCP as a fully integrated, secure, efficient, transparent and paperless process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The DCP will include the facilitation of e-payments and digital signing of documents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Users will also be able to retrieve details and check for updates with greater ease.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan has raised the point on potential fraud.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is something that SLA will consider in its design and implementation of the DCP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In terms of security, SLA will put in place robust data and cybersecurity measures, including data encryption and active monitoring of data access to detect any suspicious online activity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides benefiting buyers and sellers, the DCP will make it more efficient for those involved in the conveyancing process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will be a tool that assists lawyers, financial institutions, real estate agents and developers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Responding to Mr Zhulkarnain, SLA had extensively engaged stakeholders since 2019 and will continue to do so at each stage of the DCP's development to ensure that the end product meets the needs of all parties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Given the high value nature of property transactions, this serves as a safeguard of the individual's interests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Nevertheless, such digitalisation projects will naturally, over time, result in less emphasis being placed on certain processes or skillsets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The development brings value to the larger community by making processes simpler and faster.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Hence, we encourage conveyancing practices to adapt to, innovate and leverage on the DCP to deliver better service to their clients.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have a last section and would gratefully request for your indulgence for a bit more.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Please take a few minutes to round up.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Geospatial technology has transformative potential on the way we live, work and play.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This can unlock opportunities to benefit businesses and citizens and enable sustainability efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin will be happy to hear that SLA has been actively engaging the industry, institutions and community to mainstream the use of geospatial capabilities, promote greater awareness and understanding of their potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Through these MOUs, geospatial data and platforms, including OneMap, will be leveraged to benefit their members and customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These include enhancing building design, operations and maintenance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the science and environment community, SLA started partnerships with various agencies to deepen the use of geospatial data for weather monitoring, coastal protection, flood mitigation, carbon-sink estimation and climate studies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SLA will also be exploring how geospatial elements can be introduced in the education curriculum.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One such initiative is the Global Navigation Satellite Systems Innovation Challenge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With our limited land, it is integral that we continue to find creative ways to optimise our space in a sustainable manner to meet the needs of our community and economic demand.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We thank Mr Cheng Hsing Yao for suggesting an overarching plan for the interim use of state land.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For 2022, we partnered with stakeholders and the public to enhance various State lands and properties, such as the rejuvenation of Gillman Barracks and the development of a new three-generation park at Yarrow Gardens.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This year, SLA will continue to rejuvenate State-owned properties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SLA will work with VIVITA Singapore, a social impact organisation that seeks to empower children and youths to be changemakers for the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Through SLA's sustained efforts over the years, we have developed the Dempsey cluster into a lifestyle destination and a place for communities to gather.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And to retain its attractiveness, SLA improved the infrastructure to make it better.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SLA will continue to enhance Dempsey and expand it into a sustainable lifestyle destination that has many offerings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Innovative concepts and sustainability initiatives will be introduced to complement the current diverse mix of lifestyle activities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Even as SLA rolls out new plans, we must balance the impact on nature and the environment – a point raised by Ms Nadia Samdin.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SLA is cognisant of the need for this balance and has upheld the rustic nature of the Southern Islands and, in general, only low-intensity development has been carried out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SLA works with various agencies, including National Parks Board (NParks), to safeguard the biodiversity and heritage of the lands even as interest and the number of visitors grows.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary, I will have to ask you to round up.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am going to remind Members we only have a few minutes, so please be succinct.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Otherwise, we cannot take too many questions, and the Minister and the Senior Parliamentary Secretary cannot respond.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Can I ask the Minister to elaborate more on the three categories of the cases eligible for mandatory mediation?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Usually, it is the nature or the cases that are most appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that would be one category of cases that we would like to put through mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also mentioned re-mediation, in the event that cases which had previously gone to mediation but were not successful in maintaining the mediated position for a period of time, and new issues arise related to the mediated agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also intend to make mediation the first port of call – something that will be required before a party can bring a case to the CDRT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for this is because, as I mentioned earlier, we want to drive the parties' behaviour towards mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The best thing to do is to say that you should not be using CDRT resources, which really should be reserved as a measure of last resort, without trying the mediation process first.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will, in the context of shaping the framework, be more specific about how they will be implemented in conjunction with the specific rules for mediation, and also the CDRT process and the rules for filing a CDRT claim.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: The deferment of the admission regime changes from 2023 to 2024 has caused some junior lawyers and law graduates some anxiety.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: For example, is it due to an urgent need for young lawyers to be called?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Is there a rough indication of when that might be?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: My second clarification to Senior Parliamentary Secretary is on the Southern Islands.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for that is, as I explained in my speech, we have had COVID-19 for the past two and a half years or so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think as we begin to open up, the firm processes for working from home and arrangements with the supervision of their trainees have been re-adjusted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we thought, given feedback from the firms, that it is better to let these practices settle because the way in which trainees work in the firms, how they interact with their seniors, with their mentors, with the senior lawyers, is going to be a key part of that training and a key part of that expansion of the one year.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We wanted to let these new post-COVID-19 work processes settle before we implement the changes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As to when it will come onstream, it will be shortly – certainly, ahead of time and in good time for the trainees to be kept informed of the timeline and the arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But really, there is no change in the regime at all.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At this juncture, we are balancing the needs and if there are any further developments, we will make the announcement accordingly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But I would like to assure you that even as we are rolling out new plans, we are very conscious of taking necessary measures to make sure that we are protecting the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This includes safeguarding areas for conservation and research activities, like the Small Sister's Island; and areas for public recreation, such as lodges, campsites and beaches at St John's Island, Lazarus Island and Pulau Hantu.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Can the Ministry assure us that even as there are new measures which are digital, which are online, that these processors will remain accessible to older Singaporeans who may not be as English literate as their younger counterparts?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I can appreciate that that is of concern to that generation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But as I mentioned earlier, there are actually many different avenues of support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also have the support available to give legal advice and assistance, also, within the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, I hope that people in the community can leverage on those services as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But nonetheless, their plans for 2023 are clearly spelled out.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wish them well – as well as their colleagues in MinLaw – in really pursuing the mission of providing access to justice and maintaining the rule of law.
